rewrites.summary:
Angola demands real caution from trans visitors. The 2020 Penal Code decriminalised same-sex conduct AND prohibited discrimination based on sexual orientation — one of Africa's stronger statutory packages on paper. A 2024 shadow report by Angolan LGBT organisations (Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, Movimento T and others) documents the gap: discrimination persists across health, education and employment; trans people have no legal gender recognition; and violence goes under-investigated. Luanda has a visible, organised community.

If a trans visitor is arrested, the consequence axis is largely undocumented: the 2024 shadow report — the only prison-axis source in this record — contains no data on where trans prisoners are housed in Angola (nothing on birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, or solitary/segregation practice). Its closest custody finding is the June 2024 case of a transgender woman in Viana (Luanda) attacked by police because of her gender identity, physically injured, arbitrarily detained and subjected to degrading treatment (under investigation by the judicial military police of the Provincial Command of Luanda; police custody, no prison-placement information). In a legal system with no gender recognition and under-investigated violence, an undocumented placement practice cannot be assumed safe: what is on record is police violence against a trans person in custody.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Same-sex conduct is decriminalised and sexual-orientation discrimination prohibited — of direct concern mainly to trans visitors who have relationships or are perceived as same-sex-active while travelling.

Legal context: the 2020 Penal Code that decriminalised same-sex conduct also criminalises discrimination based on sexual orientation with up to two years' imprisonment — a statutory sanction the same 2024 report documents as failing to stop persistent discrimination in health, education and employment.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Trans people have no legal gender recognition; the implementation gap (health, education, employment discrimination, under-investigated violence) falls on residents.

The June 2024 Viana incident is a residents' case: a transgender woman attacked by police because of her gender identity, physically injured, arbitrarily detained by Esquadra 43 and subjected to degrading treatment, with the case under investigation by the judicial military police of the Provincial Command of Luanda — police custody with no prison-placement information produced.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Statutory protections vs implementation gap documented by Angolan CSOs.

Prison axis: no Angolan rule, case or practice is documented on trans-prisoner housing — no birth-sex vs identity placement finding, no trans special units, no solitary/segregation practice; the June 2024 case ended in police custody rather than prison placement, and what happens to trans people held after charge is unrecorded in these sources.
rewrites.notes: rw002 VIS: folded verified prison-axis source (2024 shadow report: no placement practice documented; June 2024 Viana police detention of a trans woman) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Antigua and Barbuda demands real caution. The High Court struck down the buggery/gross-indecency laws in July 2022, reading the constitutional bar on sex discrimination to cover sexual orientation and gender identity. No LGR, no anti-discrimination statute, and residual social hostility; tourist resort areas are insulated.

The consequence axis of an arrest is undocumented: the Outright International profile (page states 'Last Update: March 12, 2026') contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement — no birth-sex vs identity rule, no trans special units, no solitary/segregation practice — in a state with no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination statute, where the profile itself records transgender people as particularly vulnerable because no legal gender recognition mechanism exists; a detained trans visitor would face a prison system with no documented housing standard for trans people, and the absence of any rule cannot be read as a protected one.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
The 2022 decriminalisation ruling covers same-sex conduct — relevant to trans visitors travelling with a partner; the criminal statutes no longer apply to anyone.

Litigation and legal-flux context: the 2022 ruling struck down Sections 12 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1995 and read the constitutional bar on sex discrimination as inclusive of sexual orientation and gender identity; same-sex unions remain unrecognised, so partner-related protection stops at criminal-law neutrality, and no explicit anti-discrimination protections have followed the ruling.
rewrites.localsOnly:
No legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination statute — resident-facing gaps.

For residents the gaps are concrete: there is no mechanism to change legal gender markers (only name changes), and the Outright profile records transgender people as particularly vulnerable because of that absence.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Decriminalisation is recent; social climate lags the courts.

Prison axis: no Antigua and Barbuda data on trans-prisoner housing placement (birth-sex vs identity), special units or solitary/segregation practice is documented in any source in this record; the gap cannot be read as safe in a state with no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination statute.
rewrites.notes: rw002 VIS: folded verified prison-axis source (Outright profile: 2022 ruling affirmed; no placement practice documented) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Australia is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court’s landmark Tickle v Giggle ruling confirmed that gender-identity discrimination protection covers trans women as women — with compensation awarded. States have modernised rapidly: Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections (April 2024) and NSW, another state, passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction; and marriage equality has held since 2017 (relevant to same-sex partners travelling together).

Counterweights: the Tickle case itself arose from organised exclusionary activism, which is vocal in Australia; ANROWS research documents systemic discrimination and harassment of trans people; and a NSW court granted a trans woman an apprehended-violence order against a Binary Australia activist who had targeted her — real harassment, but also functioning legal recourse.

For a visitor: full legal protection and functioning courts; low incident probability; border and document-screening practice is not detailed in the current sources. The consequence axis of an arrest is documented at state level in Queensland: under the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022 (fully in force 2023) and its August 2023 inspection standards, transgender and intersex prisoners are generally to be admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender — identity-based placement — but staff still hold discretion at admission, and only transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that process; the 2009 Corrective Services procedure this oversight replaced was assessed as largely ineffective. Placement practice in the other states is not detailed in the current sources.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Adjacent context: the national legal trend is settled and protective — federal sex-discrimination protection (2013), the 2024 federal court reading of it, and rapid state modernisation — while the live policy pressure documented nationally is the organised exclusionary campaign landscape (facilities and records-access disputes, rights-rollback pressures).

History and framing: state-by-state decriminalisation unfolded over decades from laws inherited from the historic metropole (one state kept the death penalty until 1949), and the national protections debate includes an ongoing terminological dispute over whether intersex people belong inside the same framework — framing, not visitor-facing risk. A federal hate-crime offence (2025) and conversion-therapy bans covering most of the population (2024) extend the protective layer beyond the earlier baseline.

Policy evolution behind the placement standard: the 2009 Queensland Corrective Services procedure on transgender prisoners was assessed as largely ineffective (Jenny Samiec, Queensland Law Student Review 2009), and oversight shifted to the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022 — institutional history rather than a visitor-facing risk.
rewrites.localsOnly:
State-level legal gender recognition remains a patchwork (only some jurisdictions are self-declaration) and healthcare access gaps are resident-facing.

Resident-facing discrimination data from the sources: a 2003 research brief documented trans people’s difficulties with sex designations on identity documents (passports, licences and birth certificates), high job-loss rates around transition, and greater exposure to assault and harassment in public places; the 2024 state-law modernisations (Queensland, NSW) govern residents, not visitors.

The Queensland custody rules are resident-facing: placement by lived or experienced gender with staff discretion at admission and a surgery exception governs prisoners, not visitors; a visitor meets it only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
State-level legal gender recognition patchwork and healthcare access gaps are resident-facing; the current sources do not assess marriage or partner-travel questions beyond the 2017 marriage-equality baseline, and border-document screening practice for visitors is not detailed.

Unverifiable in the current sources: three of the seven listed sources were not retrievable at research time (access denied; page removed; assembly bill text), including the 2024 discrimination ruling report and a state bill text; the remaining assessment of organised campaigns rests on the research brief alone.

Prison axis: the placement finding is Queensland-only and rests on a single Wikipedia section; no data in these sources documents trans-prisoner housing in the other states, special units, or solitary/segregation practice, and how the surgery exclusion is applied in practice is not documented.
rewrites.notes: rw002 VIS: folded verified prison-axis source (Wikipedia LGBTQ people in prison — Queensland identity-based placement with admission discretion and surgery exception; 2009 procedure assessed ineffective) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Belize demands real caution. The Court of Appeal struck down the sodomy law in 2016 (Orozco v AG) — the Caribbean's first decriminalisation ruling; Belize has an organised community (UNIBAM) and anti-discrimination employment protection. No LGR; gang violence in Belize City is a general risk.

The consequence axis of an arrest is undocumented: the one prison-axis source in this record — the Wikipedia survey of LGBTQ people in prison — returns no usable finding for Belize (no birth-sex vs identity housing rule, no trans special units, and no solitary/segregation practice recorded), so where a detained trans visitor would be housed is simply unknown; with no legal gender recognition, the absence of any documented placement standard cannot be read as a protected one.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
The 2016 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

Regional framing: the 2016 Orozco ruling was the region's first decriminalisation ruling, and at the country's 2018 UN human-rights review it accepted 15 of 17 SOGI recommendations — the first CARICOM member to accept that many — pledging legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, police training and SOGI data collection, with two rights-equality recommendations noted rather than accepted.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
No LGR; Belize City violence is general.

Prison axis: the only prison-axis source (the Wikipedia survey, fetched HTTP 200) is thin for Belize — it records no birth-sex vs identity housing rule, no trans special units and no solitary/segregation practice for the country, and its only Belize mention is a 'Violence in Belize' navbox taxonomy link — so no usable placement finding exists, and that absence is the finding, not a signal of safety.
rewrites.notes: rw002 VIS: folded verified prison-axis source (Wikipedia survey: thin for Belize, no usable placement finding) into visible fields as thin-data consequence evidence per LANE_SPECS rule 8b; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Brazil combines some of the world's strongest legal protections for transgender people with a high level of real-world violence — the classic gap between law and practice. Courts allow name and gender-marker changes without surgery, the Supreme Court has criminalised transphobia (making it punishable like racism), courts fine businesses that discriminate, and official guidance affirms trans people's right to use bathrooms matching their identity.

For visitors, big-city queer life is vibrant and highly visible — São Paulo hosts the world's largest Pride parade — and the law is unambiguously on a trans traveller's side. The practical risks are concentrated in nightlife and app-based meetings: a majority of physical violence against LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo happens at night, and robbery schemes luring gay men via dating apps have been fatal.

Exercise particular caution after dark, with nightlife and app meetings, and in peripheral areas. Violence against local trans people (Brazil records the world's highest absolute toll) is heavily concentrated in poor and marginalised communities, not tourist areas. The consequence axis if a trans visitor is arrested is a documented law-practice gap: under the National Council of Justice's Resolution 348 (13 Oct 2020, amended 2021) a person is recognised as LGBTI for custody purposes by self-declaration before a judge, the judge fixes the place of detention in a reasoned decision after consulting the person's preference, must inform them of the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit and within it the general population or specific wings or cells, records the declared preference (with transfers prioritised in cases of violence or serious threat), and may not use LGBTI-specific spaces as disciplinary isolation; yet the only state-level census in these sources — 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates interviewed inside eleven units treated as masculine across Rio de Janeiro state (April–June 2021) — found them housed in masculine units, some in 'neutral' or 'security' units, with male-unit placement documented as a double punishment amid recurring basic-rights violations.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Dating-app robbery schemes (documented as fatal for gay men) are a caution for trans visitors using apps.

Custody framework context: the national placement framework (CNJ Resolution 348/2020, amended 2021) is judiciary-level machinery rather than a visitor-facing protection, and the census documenting birth-sex practice was produced with a lead author inside the LGBTI health division of Rio de Janeiro's state penitentiary administration — the gap between norm and practice is documented from inside the system.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The name/gender-marker change procedure and the transphobia criminalisation are resident-facing legal machinery; the world's-highest trans murder toll falls on local trans people, concentrated in poor and marginalised communities.

The custody practice is resident-facing: the Rio de Janeiro state census (138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates interviewed in eleven units treated as masculine, April–June 2021) documents travestis and trans women housed in masculine units, some in 'neutral' or 'security' units, with male-unit placement framed as a double punishment amid recurring basic-rights violations; state law has since 2015 granted them parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units (hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics), and the national norms let them be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine — a visitor meets all of it only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Brazil's general crime problem (armed robbery, express kidnappings, gang violence) drives all governments to advise a high degree of caution for every traveller.

Prison axis: enforcement of the CNJ framework is documented only to the extent of the one Rio de Janeiro state census (2021); no source in this record tracks whether other states follow the Resolution's consultation and placement rules, and no data on solitary or segregation practice for trans prisoners appears — the ban on using LGBTI-specific spaces as disciplinary isolation is the norm on paper (Art. 11, VI–VII), not documented practice.
rewrites.notes: rw002 VIS: folded 2 verified prison-axis sources (CNJ Resolution 348/2020 national placement framework; 2024 Rio census finding masculine-unit housing) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.
